units.title: Hello, Ruby
units.summary: Write your first Ruby programs: print text and numbers with puts, print and p, and let Ruby calculate.

lesson.md: Ruby is a programming language that is easy to read. A Ruby program is a list of instructions. The computer runs them from top to bottom, one line after the other. Your first instruction is `puts`: it prints a value and then starts a new line.

lesson.code: puts "Hello, Ruby!"

lesson.md: Text in quotes is called a **string**. You can write it with double quotes, `"Hi"`, or with single quotes, `'Hi'`. Every `puts` prints its own line.

lesson.code:
puts "Hello"
puts 'World'
puts "Ruby is fun"

lesson.md: Numbers need no quotes. Ruby calculates with `+` (plus), `-` (minus), `*` (times) and `/` (divided by). Whole numbers are called **integers**. When you divide two integers, Ruby drops the part after the decimal point: `7 / 2` is `3`. Write `7.0 / 2` to get `3.5`. `%` gives the remainder of a division: `7 % 2` is `1`.

lesson.code:
puts 2 + 3
puts 10 - 4
puts 3 * 4
puts 7 / 2
puts 7.0 / 2
puts 7 % 2

lesson.md: Quotes make a big difference. `"2"` with quotes is text, `2` without quotes is a number. `+` between two strings joins them, and `+` between two numbers adds them.

lesson.code:
puts "2" + "3"
puts 2 + 3

lesson.md: `print` prints a value **without** a new line at the end, so the next output continues on the same line. `p` prints a value the way Ruby sees it: a string keeps its quotes. Programmers use `p` to check values while they work.

lesson.code:
print "Hello, "
print "World"
puts "!"
p "Ruby"
p 42

lesson.md: Everything after a `#` on a line is a **comment**. Ruby ignores it. In this course, comments only show results, for example `puts 2 + 3 # 5`.

card: `puts "Hi"` prints and starts a new line
`p "Hi"` shows the value as Ruby sees it: `"Hi"`

`"2"` and `"3"` are strings because of the quotes. `+` joins two strings, so the result is `23`.

units.title: Variables and types
units.summary: Store values in variables, meet Integer, Float, String, true, false and nil, and put values into text with #{}.

lesson.md: A **variable** is a name for a value. You create it with `=`: the name on the left, the value on the right. After that, you use the name instead of the value.

lesson.code:
name = "Mia"
age = 12
puts name
puts age

lesson.md: A variable can get a new value later; Ruby then forgets the old one. `score += 5` is short for `score = score + 5`, and `score -= 1` is short for `score = score - 1`. Variable names use small letters and underscores, like `first_name`.

lesson.code:
score = 10
puts score
score = score + 5
puts score
score += 1
puts score
score -= 6
puts score

lesson.md: Every value has a type, which Ruby calls its **class**. `.class` asks a value for its class. Whole numbers are `Integer`, numbers with a decimal point are `Float`, and text is `String`. `true` and `false` answer yes-or-no questions. `nil` means "no value".

lesson.code:
puts 42.class
puts 3.14.class
puts "hi".class
puts true.class
puts false.class
puts nil.class
lesson.output:
Integer
Float
String
TrueClass
FalseClass
NilClass

lesson.md: `puts nil` prints an empty line, because `nil` has no text. `p nil` shows `nil`.
To put a value into a string, write `#{}` inside **double quotes** and put a variable or a calculation between the braces. This is called **interpolation**. It does not work with single quotes.

lesson.code:
name = "Mia"
age = 12
puts "#{name} is #{age} years old."
puts "Next year: #{age + 1}"
puts 'No #{name} here'
lesson.output:
Mia is 12 years old.
Next year: 13
No #{name} here

lesson.md: You cannot join a string and a number with `+`: `"Age: " + 12` stops with an error (`TypeError`). Convert the value first. `.to_s` turns a value into a string, `.to_i` turns a string into an integer, and `.to_f` turns it into a float.

lesson.code:
age = 12
puts "Age: " + age.to_s
puts "5".to_i + 3
puts "2.5".to_f * 2

card: `"Hi #{name}"` puts a value into a string (double quotes only)

units.title: Strings
units.summary: Change and check text with string methods like upcase, length, include? and gsub, and take parts of a string.

lesson.md: A **method** is an action that a value can do. You call it with a dot after the value, like `"hello".upcase`. `upcase` gives the text in capital letters, `downcase` in small letters, and `capitalize` makes only the first letter a capital.

lesson.code:
word = "ruby"
puts word.upcase
puts "HELLO".downcase
puts "hello world".capitalize

lesson.md: `length` counts the characters of a string; spaces count too. `reverse` gives the characters in reverse order.

lesson.code:
puts "Ruby".length
puts "Hi there".length
puts "stressed".reverse

lesson.md: Some methods need extra information. You pass it in parentheses `()`; it is called an **argument**. A method name that ends with `?` answers a question with `true` or `false`. `include?` checks if a string contains some text, `start_with?` and `end_with?` check the beginning and the end, and `empty?` checks if a string has no characters.

lesson.code:
text = "I like Ruby"
puts text.include?("Ruby")
puts text.include?("ruby")
puts text.start_with?("I")
puts text.end_with?("!")
puts "".empty?

lesson.md: `gsub(a, b)` replaces **every** `a` with `b`. `sub(a, b)` replaces only the first one. `strip` removes spaces at the start and the end. You can call one method after the other: `"  hi  ".strip.upcase` first removes the spaces, then makes capitals.

lesson.code:
text = "one two one"
puts text.gsub("one", "1")
puts text.sub("one", "1")
puts "  hi  ".strip.upcase

lesson.md: These methods return a **new** string; the original stays the same. Store the result if you need it: `word = word.upcase`.

lesson.code:
word = "ruby"
loud = word.upcase
puts word
puts loud

lesson.md: Each character has a position, called its **index**. The first index is `0`, not `1`. `word[0]` is the first character and `word[-1]` is the last one. `word[start, count]` takes `count` characters, beginning at index `start`.

lesson.code:
word = "Ruby"
puts word[0]
puts word[1]
puts word[-1]
puts word[0, 2]
puts word[1, 3]

card: `s[0]` is the first character, `s[-1]` the last, `s[1, 3]` three from index 1

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Let your program choose with if, elsif, else and unless, compare values, combine conditions and use case and when.

lesson.md: A comparison gives `true` or `false`. `==` checks if two values are equal; remember that one `=` stores a value and two compare. `!=` means "not equal". `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=` mean less than, greater than, less or equal, and greater or equal.

lesson.code:
age = 15
puts age == 15
puts age != 15
puts age > 18
puts age <= 15

lesson.md: `if` runs code only when its condition is `true`. The code after `else` runs when it is `false`. `end` closes the whole block. Indent the code inside by two spaces: Ruby does not need it, but it makes the code easy to read.

lesson.code:
temperature = 25
if temperature > 20
  puts "Warm"
else
  puts "Cold"
end

lesson.md: `elsif` checks another condition when the ones before it were `false`. Ruby tests the conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first branch that matches.

lesson.code:
score = 75
if score >= 90
  puts "A"
elsif score >= 70
  puts "B"
else
  puts "C"
end

lesson.md: `&&` means **and**: both sides must be `true`. `||` means **or**: one true side is enough. `!` turns `true` into `false` and `false` into `true`. `unless` is the opposite of `if`: its code runs when the condition is `false`.

lesson.code:
age = 20
ticket = true
if age >= 18 && ticket
  puts "Welcome"
end
unless ticket
  puts "Buy a ticket"
end
puts age < 12 || age > 65
puts !ticket

lesson.md: For one short line, you can put `if` or `unless` at the end: `puts "Hot" if temperature > 30`. The **ternary operator** `condition ? a : b` gives `a` when the condition is `true` and `b` when it is `false`.

lesson.code:
temperature = 35
puts "Hot" if temperature > 30
puts "Freezing" if temperature < 0
label = temperature > 20 ? "warm" : "cold"
puts label

lesson.md: `case` compares one value with several options. Each `when` lists one or more values, separated by commas. The code after `else` runs when no `when` matches.

lesson.code:
day = "Sat"
case day
when "Sat", "Sun"
  puts "Weekend"
when "Fri"
  puts "Almost weekend"
else
  puts "Workday"
end

lesson.md: In Ruby, only `false` and `nil` count as false in a condition. Every other value counts as true, even `0` and the empty string `""`.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?

exercises.explain: `7 > 5` is `true`, so the `if` branch runs.

exercises.explain: Only `false` and `nil` count as false in Ruby. `0` counts as true, so the `if` branch runs.

units.title: Loops and ranges
units.summary: Repeat code with times, each, upto and while, and count through ranges like 1..5.

lesson.md: A **loop** repeats code. The easiest loop in Ruby is `times`: `3.times` runs the code three times. The code between `do` and `end` is called a **block**.

lesson.code:
3.times do
  puts "Hello"
end

lesson.md: A block can receive a value between two bars, like `|i|`. With `times`, `i` counts from `0`. For short blocks, you can use curly braces `{ }` instead of `do` and `end`.

lesson.code:
3.times do |i|
  puts "Round #{i}"
end
2.times { puts "Hi" }

lesson.md: A **range** is a sequence of values from a start to an end. `1..5` contains 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. With three dots, `1...5` stops **before** the end: 1, 2, 3 and 4. `each` runs a block once for every value. Ranges also have methods: `sum` adds all values, and `include?` checks if a value is part of the range.

lesson.code:
(1..3).each do |n|
  puts n * 10
end
numbers = 1...5
puts numbers.sum
puts numbers.include?(5)

lesson.md: `upto` counts up from one number to another, and `downto` counts down.
A `while` loop repeats its code as long as its condition is `true`. Make sure that the code in the loop changes the condition; otherwise, the loop never stops.

lesson.code:
count = 1
while count <= 3
  puts "Count: #{count}"
  count += 1
end
puts "Done"

lesson.md: `break` leaves a loop at once. `next` skips the rest of the block and continues with the next value. `n.even?` is `true` for even numbers, and `n.odd?` for odd numbers.

lesson.code:
(1..10).each do |n|
  next if n.even?
  break if n > 7
  puts n
end

card: `(1..5).each do |n| … end` runs once for every value

units.title: Methods
units.summary: Write your own methods with def, give them parameters and default values, and return results.

lesson.md: A **method** is a named piece of code that you can run again and again. You define it with `def`, a name, the code, and `end`. You **call** the method by writing its name.

lesson.code:
def greet
  puts "Hello!"
end

greet
greet

lesson.md: **Parameters** are variables in parentheses after the method name. When you call the method, you give it values for them; these values are the **arguments**. Separate several parameters with commas.

lesson.code:
def greet(name)
  puts "Hello, #{name}!"
end

greet("Ana")
greet("Ben")

lesson.md: A parameter can have a **default value**: `def greet(name = "friend")`. When you call the method without an argument, Ruby uses the default.

lesson.code:
def greet(name = "friend")
  puts "Hello, #{name}!"
end

greet("Ana")
greet

lesson.md: A method gives back a value, its **return value**: the value of the last line that runs. You do not need to write `return` for it. Use `return` to leave a method early with a value.

lesson.code:
def add(a, b)
  a + b
end

def sign(n)
  return "negative" if n < 0
  "positive or zero"
end

puts add(2, 3)
puts sign(-4)
puts sign(7)

lesson.md: Methods that answer a yes-or-no question end with `?` and return `true` or `false`, like `even?`. You can name your own methods the same way.

lesson.code:
def adult?(age)
  age >= 18
end

puts adult?(20)
puts adult?(12)
puts 10.even?

lesson.md: A method that ends with `!` usually changes the value itself instead of returning a new one. `upcase` returns a new string; `upcase!` changes the string that is stored in the variable.

lesson.code:
name = "ruby"
puts name.upcase
puts name
name.upcase!
puts name

lesson.md: A variable that you create outside a method does not exist inside it, and the other way round. Give values to a method as arguments, and get results back as the return value.

card: The last line gives the return value; `return` leaves early
`?` methods answer yes or no; `!` methods change the value

exercises.explain: The last line of the method, `n * 2`, is its return value: 21 times 2 is 42.

units.title: Arrays and hashes
units.summary: Keep many values in arrays and hashes, use symbols as keys, and work with each, map, select and sum.

lesson.md: An **array** is an ordered list of values in square brackets `[]`, separated by commas. Each element has an index, starting at `0`, like the characters of a string. `p` shows the whole array.

lesson.code:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
puts fruits[0]
puts fruits[-1]
puts fruits.length
p fruits

lesson.md: `<<` adds an element at the end. `first` and `last` give the first and the last element, `include?` checks if a value is in the array, and `sort` returns a sorted copy.

lesson.code:
numbers = [5, 2, 8]
numbers << 1
p numbers
puts numbers.first
puts numbers.include?(8)
p numbers.sort

lesson.md: `each` runs a block for every element. `map` builds a new array from the results of the block. `select` keeps only the elements for which the block gives `true`. `sum`, `min` and `max` work on arrays of numbers.
`join` turns an array into one string. Its argument goes between the elements: `["a", "b", "c"].join(", ")` gives `a, b, c`.

A **hash** stores pairs of a **key** and a **value** in curly braces `{}`. You get a value with its key in square brackets. Keys are often **symbols**: names with a colon in front, like `:name`. A symbol is a fixed label. In a hash, `name: "Ana"` is short for the key `:name` with the value `"Ana"`.

lesson.code:
person = { name: "Ana", age: 30 }
puts person[:name]
puts person[:age]
person[:city] = "Lima"
puts person[:city]
puts person.length
p person.keys

lesson.md: Keys can also be strings; then you write `=>` between the key and the value. A key that is not in the hash gives `nil`. `each` on a hash gives the block two values: the key and the value.

lesson.code:
prices = { "apple" => 2, "pear" => 3 }
p prices["kiwi"]
prices.each do |fruit, price|
  puts "#{fruit}: #{price}"
end

lesson.md: `:name` and `"name"` are different keys. If you store a value with the symbol `:name`, you must also read it with `:name`.

card: `:name` is a symbol; a missing key gives `nil`

units.title: Classes
units.summary: Build your own kinds of objects with class, initialize and instance variables, and add methods, attr_accessor and to_s.

lesson.md: Everything in Ruby is an **object**, and every object belongs to a **class**: `"hi"` is an object of the class `String`. A class is like a blueprint. You define your own class with `class`, a name that starts with a capital letter, and `end`. `new` creates an object of the class.

lesson.code:
class Dog
  def bark
    "Woof!"
  end
end

rex = Dog.new
puts rex.bark
puts rex.class

lesson.md: `initialize` is a special method: `new` calls it when it creates an object, and passes on its arguments. A variable that starts with `@` is an **instance variable**. Each object has its own copy, and all methods of the object can use it.

lesson.code:
class Dog
  def initialize(name)
    @name = name
  end

  def bark
    "#{@name} says Woof!"
  end
end

rex = Dog.new("Rex")
bello = Dog.new("Bello")
puts rex.bark
puts bello.bark
lesson.output:
Rex says Woof!
Bello says Woof!

lesson.md: Code outside the class cannot read instance variables: `rex.name` does not work yet. `attr_reader :name` adds a method `name` that returns `@name`. `attr_accessor :age` adds a method to read `@age` and one to change it with `=`.

lesson.code:
class Dog
  attr_reader :name
  attr_accessor :age

  def initialize(name, age)
    @name = name
    @age = age
  end
end

rex = Dog.new("Rex", 3)
puts rex.name
rex.age = 4
puts rex.age

lesson.md: Methods can change instance variables. This way, every object keeps its own **state**.

lesson.code:
class Counter
  attr_reader :count

  def initialize
    @count = 0
  end

  def increment
    @count += 1
  end
end

a = Counter.new
b = Counter.new
a.increment
a.increment
b.increment
puts a.count
puts b.count

lesson.md: `puts` calls the method `to_s` to turn an object into text, and interpolation with `#{}` does the same. Define `to_s` in your class to decide what your objects look like as text.

lesson.code:
class Point
  def initialize(x, y)
    @x = x
    @y = y
  end

  def to_s
    "(#{@x}, #{@y})"
  end
end

point = Point.new(2, 5)
puts point
puts "Point: #{point}"

lesson.md: Without your own `to_s`, `puts` prints something like `#<Point:0x000…>`: the class name and a memory address.

card: `@name` is an instance variable: each object has its own

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
class Cat
  def initialize(name)
    @name = name
  end

  def greet
    "Meow, I am #{@name}"
  end
end

puts Cat.new("Tom").greet
exercises.explain: `new` passes `"Tom"` to `initialize`, which stores it in `@name`. `greet` uses `@name`.

exercises.prompt: Which method does `new` call when it creates an object?
exercises.explain: `new` creates the object and then calls its `initialize` method with the arguments.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
class Counter
  attr_reader :count

  def initialize
    @count = 10
  end

  def add(n)
    @count += n
  end
end

c = Counter.new
c.add(5)
c.add(1)
puts c.count
exercises.explain: `@count` starts at 10. The two calls add 5 and 1, so it ends at 16.
The class has no method `name`, so the call stops with an error (`NoMethodError`). Add `attr_reader :name` to the class to fix it.

light.switch

exercises.explain: `@on` starts as `false`. Each `switch` flips it: true, false, true.
